mcqs.question: Where is a file's name actually stored in a Unix file system?
options: Inside the inode itself, as a dedicated name field
In the file's first data block, as a header
In the file system's superblock, alongside the inode count
In the directory entry that maps a name to an inode number — the inode has no name field
mcqs.explanation: Inodes hold metadata and block pointers but never a name — names live only in directory entries. This is precisely what makes hard links possible: two directory entries, same inode, no naming conflict at the inode level.

mcqs.question: With 12 direct pointers and 4KB blocks, why does a classic Unix inode also need indirect pointers instead of just adding more direct pointers?
options: More direct pointers would make the inode's fixed size grow proportionally with the maximum file size it needs to support
The kernel legally cannot have more than 12 pointers of any kind
Indirect pointers are faster to read than direct pointers
Direct pointers only work for read-only files
mcqs.explanation: Indirect pointers let the inode stay a small, fixed size while still reaching huge files — each indirection level multiplies addressable space roughly 1024x per extra disk read, rather than requiring thousands of direct pointer slots that would bloat every inode, even for tiny files.

mcqs.question: A symbolic link can point to a path that doesn't exist yet, and the link itself remains valid. Why is this possible?
options: A symlink stores a path string, not a reference to an inode — resolution (and any failure) happens at access time, not creation time
The kernel pre-creates the target automatically
Symlinks are only checked once, at creation time
Symlinks silently fall back to an empty file if the target is missing
mcqs.explanation: A symlink's inode holds a path string. Creating it never touches the target, so a missing target doesn't make the link invalid — only trying to open it triggers resolution, which is when a missing target surfaces as an error.

mcqs.question: Why can't a hard link point to a file on a different disk partition, while a symbolic link can?
options: Hard links are deprecated on modern file systems
A hard link references an inode number, which is only meaningful within the file system that assigned it; a symlink just stores a path string that any file system can resolve
Symbolic links copy the data, so partition boundaries don't matter
Hard links require root privileges across partitions, which is usually disabled
mcqs.explanation: Inode numbers are scoped to a single file system — inode 500 on one partition has nothing to do with inode 500 on another. A symlink avoids this entirely by storing a path, which the kernel re-resolves through the normal path-lookup machinery regardless of partition boundaries.

mcqs.question: A file has two hard links, `a.txt` and `b.txt`. You run `rm a.txt`. What happens to the underlying data?
options: It's deleted immediately since rm always frees data
It becomes read-only until b.txt is also removed
Half the data blocks are freed, proportional to the link count decrease
It's fully intact and still accessible via b.txt, since the inode's link count only dropped from 2 to 1
mcqs.explanation: rm on a hard-linked file just decrements the link count and removes one name. Data is only reclaimed when the link count reaches zero and no process holds it open — with b.txt remaining, the file is fully accessible under that name.

mcqs.question: `df` shows 36GB free on a partition, but every attempt to create a new file fails with ENOSPC. What's the most likely cause?
options: The disk controller is throttling write speed
The partition has run out of inodes even though block space remains, often from millions of tiny files
The file system is corrupted and needs fsck
df is reporting stale, cached data
mcqs.explanation: Inode count is fixed at format time and tracked separately from block/space usage. A directory full of millions of tiny files can exhaust inodes while disk space usage looks fine — df -i, not df, reveals this. Corruption and stale caching are far less likely given the specific symptom.
